title: Zero-dependency Node server using node:http
context: User asked for a simple URL shortener with no stack specified; Node is installed.
options: node:http built-in: no install step, ~100 lines, manual routing
Express: nicer routing, but adds a dependency for three routes
Python Flask: equally small, but needs pip install
why: Three routes don't justify a framework; the project runs with just `npm start` and nothing to install.

title: Persist links to a JSON file rewritten on every write
context: Links need to survive restarts, but this is meant to be simple.
options: In-memory only: simplest, loses links on restart
JSON file rewritten per write: persistent, no deps, not safe for concurrent processes or large volumes
SQLite: robust, but adds a native dependency
why: Persistence with no dependencies; fine for a single-process toy. Swap for SQLite if this needs to scale.

title: Random 6-char base64url codes, only http(s) targets allowed
context: Need short codes and to avoid the shortener redirecting to dangerous schemes.
options: Sequential counter base62: shortest codes, but enumerable
Random 6-char base64url with collision retry: unguessable enough, ~68 billion space
Hash of URL: dedupes, but collisions on truncation need handling anyway
choice: Random base64url, retry on collision; reject non-http(s) URLs
why: Random codes aren't enumerable; restricting schemes blocks javascript:/data: redirects. Same URL gets a new code each time (no dedupe), which keeps it simple.

title: Redirect with 302 rather than 301
context: Short links can redirect temporarily or permanently.
options: 301 permanent: browsers cache it, fewer server hits, but a link can never be changed or removed for anyone who visited it
302 temporary: every visit goes through the server, so links stay editable and countable later
why: Keeps the option to edit, delete or count link visits later. The extra request costs nothing at this scale.

title: Accept only http: and https: target URLs
context: Split out of D3, which bundled this with code generation and was anchored on the wrong function. Raised in review.
options: Accept any string the URL parser takes: most flexible, but stores javascript:, data:, file: and app-launching schemes like ms-msdt:
Allow only http: and https:: covers every normal web link, rejects everything else
Allow https: only: stricter, but breaks plain-http sites people still link to
why: Modern browsers already refuse to follow a 302 to javascript: or data:, so this is defense in depth: it stops redirects that open local apps or files, and keeps stored URLs safe to render if a link list is added later.
